Well, thank you for fitting me in. I... I suppose I should give you a little context first so you understand where I am coming from. I’m a secondary school teacher, and I have been for quite some time, so I am very used to the daily rhythms of a school, you know, the administrative side of things, the constant communication. But lately, I’ve been dealing with something that I just can’t seem to get past, which is why I’m here. 

It really centers around the morning routine. I came in today because I simply cannot shake this intense feeling that certain staff emails and the daily morning announcements are... well, that they are actually coded messages about me. I know how unusual that might sound to say out loud. But when I sit at my desk before first period and read through the administration’s updates, the specific phrasing they use just feels so deeply personal, like there is a hidden meaning intended only for me to understand. And the announcements over the loudspeaker, the way certain words are emphasized by the principal... it just feels directed right at me, wrapped up in ordinary school business. 

My colleagues have been very sweet about it, very gentle. A few of them have even pulled up the emails on their own computers and sat down with me to show me the recipient list, trying to prove that the exact same message was sent to every single teacher in the building. And I see it, I look right at the screen and see that it went to everyone, but... I just can't shake the feeling. The feeling doesn't go away just because the mailing list is long, you know? It just sits with me all day while I'm trying to teach my classes, this nagging certainty that the message was really just for me.

Voices... well, it’s interesting that you bring that up, because I have been noticing something along those lines, and I’ve really been going back and forth on whether or not to even mention it. You see, during the school day, it is just so incredibly loud. There’s the bell, the lockers slamming, the teenagers shouting down the halls... you barely have a single moment to hear yourself think, let alone hear anything else. 

But it’s when things finally settle down that I notice it. Usually, it happens after the final bell rings and my classroom empties out. The kids rush off to catch their buses, and I’m just sitting there at my desk, maybe wiping down the whiteboard or organizing my lesson plans for the next day, and the room is completely quiet. Or even later, when I’m finally back at my house, just in the absolute quiet of my own kitchen while I'm grading papers or putting the kettle on for a cup of tea. 

In those very still, quiet moments... I will hear a woman’s voice. It’s not a mumble or a whisper, it is perfectly clear. She’ll just say my name, or she might make a very brief, short comment about exactly what I’m doing right then in that exact moment. And it is so incredibly vivid, so real, that my immediate reflex is to reply. I actually speak out loud and answer her! I'll say, "Yes, I'm over here," or "I know, I'm just finishing up," before it suddenly dawns on me that the door is shut, the house or the classroom is completely empty, and there is absolutely no one else there with me. It’s just so disorienting because of how perfectly ordinary and clear the voice sounds, you know? I always end up getting up from my desk and checking the hallway or looking out the window just to be absolutely sure, but... there's never anyone there.

Well, let me think back, because I really want to give you an accurate timeline, and it’s a bit tricky to pinpoint the exact day it all began, you know? I’m fifty-six now, and I’ve been teaching for over thirty years, so I have a very long, very stable history of just going about my business, managing my classrooms, and dealing with the administration without a second thought. I remember it was right around the time the first quarter grades were due, which is always a very hectic time of year anyway. At first, I thought maybe I was just overthinking things because of the stress of getting all the reports filed on time. But then the quarter ended, the grades were submitted, and the stress died down, but the feelings didn't. The emails kept coming, and they kept feeling so pointed, so specific to me. And the voice... well, that hasn't gone away either. So yes, I've been fifty-six this whole time, and it's been a solid four months of dealing with this day in and day out. It’s just so strange, because for fifty-five and a half years, I never experienced anything even remotely like this.

Memory or concentration... well, it's funny you ask that, because as a teacher, I am constantly having to evaluate other people's memory and concentration, you know? I'm always telling my students, "Pay attention, focus on the text, remember what we discussed on Tuesday," so I'm very hyper-aware of cognitive slips. I have to be. I have to keep track of thirty teenagers at a time, remember who has a 504 plan, who needs extra time on tests, who is allergic to peanuts... it's a lot to juggle.

But as for my own memory and concentration? No, I really haven't noticed any issues there at all. I mean, my mind feels as sharp as it ever has. I can still sit down and grade a stack of essays and spot a comma splice from a mile away. I remember all my lesson plans, I know exactly where I left off in the curriculum, and I haven't forgotten any appointments or misplaced my keys or anything like that. 

I will say, though, that the... the distractions, the voice and the emails, they certainly demand my attention. When you're sitting in a quiet room and you hear someone say your name as clear as day, it's impossible not to stop what you're doing and focus on that. So, in that exact moment, my concentration on whatever I was doing—grading, reading, making tea—is interrupted. But it's not because I've lost the ability to concentrate. It's because something very startling has just happened and pulled my focus away. Once I realize no one is there, I can sit right back down and pick up exactly where I left off. So, no, my memory is perfectly fine, and my concentration is just as good as it always is, assuming I'm not being interrupted by... well, by these things.

You see, during the school day, it is just so incredibly loud. There’s the bell, the lockers slamming, the teenagers shouting down the halls... you barely have a single moment to hear yourself think, let alone hear anything else. \n\nBut it’s when things finally settle down that I notice it. Usually, it happens after the final bell rings and my classroom empties out. Or even later, when I’m finally back at my house, just in the absolute quiet of my own kitchen while I'm grading papers or putting the kettle on for a cup of tea. \n\nIn those very still, quiet moments... She’ll just say my name, or she might make a very brief, short comment about exactly what I’m doing right then in that exact moment. And it is so incredibly vivid, so real, that my immediate reflex is to reply. I actually speak out loud and answer her! I'll say, \"Yes, I'm over here,\" or \"I know, I'm just finishing up,\" before it suddenly dawns on me that the door is shut, the house or the classroom is completely empty, and there is absolutely no one else there with me. It’s just so disorienting because of how perfectly ordinary and clear the voice sounds, you know? I always end up getting up from my desk and checking the hallway or looking out the window just to be absolutely sure, but... there's never anyone there.\n\nDoctor: Have you been having any periods of feeling unusually depressed or unusually energized or ‘up’ around the same time these experiences have been happening?\n\nPatient: Well, that's... I mean, I've really been trying to keep a close eye on my moods, you know, just as a general practice, because teaching takes so much out of you emotionally anyway. I haven't noticed anything like that. \n\nI mean, I get tired, of course. By Friday afternoon, I am just absolutely wiped out, but that's just the nature of the job, isn't it? Well, trouble keeping up... it's a complicated question, really. Because on paper, if you look at my attendance record or my grade book, I am still teaching. I haven't taken a leave of absence, I haven't called in sick... I am there every morning at 7:15, unlocking my door, turning on the smartboard, writing the day's objective on the whiteboard. I'm physically present, and I'm still delivering the curriculum. 

But... and this is hard to admit, because I pride myself on being very self-sufficient, very capable... I have had to lean on my colleagues a lot more than I usually do. Especially with the bigger project lessons. Normally, I love those. I love the chaos of thirty kids working in groups, researching, debating. But lately, with the... the emails, and the feeling that I need to be constantly monitoring the announcements and the memos for these hidden messages... the noise of a project day is just too much. It's overwhelming. So I've had to ask Mrs. Gable, and sometimes Mr. Harrison from the science department, to come in during their planning periods and just... co-facilitate, I guess you'd call it. Just to help me keep all the plates spinning while my mind is, frankly, preoccupied with trying to decipher what the administration is really saying to me. And the planning meetings, the departmental ones we have on Wednesday afternoons? I used to lead those, or at least be a very active participant. Emotionally flat... well, that’s a rather harsh way to put it, isn't it? It sounds so cold, and I want to be very clear that I am not a cold person. I still care about my students, immensely. I care about whether they understand the reading, I care about their futures, I worry about the ones who sit in the back and don't take notes. And my friends, too—I still care very deeply for my friends. 

But... well, the best way I can describe it is that for many months now, it has just felt like the warmth and the drive have completely drained out of me. Just entirely siphoned away. It’s like a battery that’s been left out in the winter, if you know what I mean. The structure is all still there, but there's no spark left to power anything.

I didn't formally resign from them, I just let them slide. I stopped showing up. And it’s not just those big commitments, either, the ones that take a lot of work. It’s even simple things, like phone calls. My sister, Brenda, she calls me from Ohio every Sunday evening, regular as clockwork. We've done this for a decade. But lately, I just sit on my sofa and watch her name flash on the caller ID until it goes to voicemail. I just don't have the... the whatever it is you need inside you to pick up the receiver and make conversation about her garden or her grandchildren. 

I just let it all slide unless someone pushes me. If Mrs. Gable doesn't physically come to my classroom at noon and say, "Come on, we are going to the staff room for lunch," I will just sit at my desk in the quiet, eating half a sandwich and staring at the wall. If someone doesn't prompt me, if someone doesn't pull me into the current, I just drift. The caring is still in my head, I know I love these people and these activities, but the actual drive to participate in my own life is just... gone.

I get my annual checkups, I take my vitamins, I try to get my steps in during my lunch break by walking the perimeter of the athletic fields if the weather is nice. \n\nBut as for anything major like a seizure or a stroke... absolutely not. I haven't hit my head, I haven't been in any accidents. The most medical trouble I've had in the last five years was a mild case of plantar fasciitis from wearing the wrong shoes on concrete floors all day, and I got orthotic inserts for that and it cleared right up. \n\nI've never been hospitalized for anything serious, never had surgery... No sudden illnesses, no fainting spells, no neurological events. Just... my perfectly ordinary, healthy life, right up until the emails started feeling so strange and the voice began. So I really don't think there's a medical, or physical, explanation for this, if that's what you're getting at. It's just my body is perfectly fine, it's just these other things that are happening.\n\nDoctor: Do you feel as though anyone or anything is controlling your thoughts, feelings, or actions?\n\nPatient: Well, controlling my thoughts or actions... no, I wouldn't say that anyone is controlling me. I still make my own decisions, I still grade my papers, I still choose what tea to drink. I'm very much in control of myself. Very routine, right? But the way certain words were phrased, the specific cadence of the sentences... it felt like a direct commentary on how I had been standing outside my door during third period. It felt like a warning, or a message meant only for my eyes, disguised as a mass email. \n\nAnd I've tried to be rational about it. I really have. I even sat down with Mrs. Gable—she teaches history across the hall, we've been friends for years—and I showed her the email. I pointed out the phrasing, and she very gently, very kindly, pulled up the exact same email on her own computer to show me that it went to everyone, word for word. She tried to assure me it was just a general reminder. And intellectually, looking at her screen, I understood what she was saying. But the feeling... that absolute certainty that the message was secretly meant for me, that it was a code I was supposed to decipher... it just wouldn't go away. It hasn't gone away. It's like I'm living in two different realities—the one where it's a normal school day, and the one where the announcements are narrating my life. It's overwhelming. So I've had to ask Mrs. Gable, and sometimes Mr. Harrison from the science department, to come in during their planning periods and just... co-facilitate, I guess you'd call it. Just to help me keep all the plates spinning while my mind is, frankly, preoccupied with trying to decipher what the administration is really saying to me. Thoughts being put into my mind? Or taken out? Oh, no, no, it’s nothing like that. It isn't like some science fiction movie where someone is tampering with my brain or stealing my memories. My thoughts are entirely my own, I assure you. I know exactly what I am thinking.

But lately, for these past few months, I have this overwhelming conviction that certain staff emails and those morning announcements are actually coded messages specifically about me. 

It sounds absurd when I say it out loud, I know it does, because I am a logical person. But when I'm sitting there reading a seemingly mundane email from the administration about, say, hallway pass procedures or faculty meeting agendas, I can read between the lines and see that it’s actually a disguised message directed entirely at me. I've even brought it up at work. I went next door to Sarah—she teaches sophomore English—and I showed her one of the emails, trying to explain the hidden meaning I was seeing. And she was so sweet, she very gently turned her monitor around and showed me her own inbox to prove that the exact same message was sent to the entire staff directory. She was trying to be helpful, gently showing me that everyone got it, that it was just a mass email. 

But even seeing it right there on her screen... it didn't change anything for me. I just couldn't shake the feeling that the message was still secretly meant for me, like I was the only one supposed to understand the real meaning behind the words. It just completely takes over my mind, trying to decode what they are saying about me in those announcements, even when all the logical evidence says otherwise. That routine is absolutely set in stone. \n\nI haven't added any new herbal things or strange vitamins, either. My sister, Brenda, the one in Ohio I mentioned earlier? She is always reading these health blogs online and trying to mail me things... oh, ashwagandha or turmeric gummies, or whatever the latest fad is, telling me they'll give me more energy or help me feel more engaged. But I always tell her, \"Brenda, I don't want to be messing with my system with unregulated supplements.\" I just don't trust them. So those bottles just sit in the back of my pantry, still sealed. I haven't touched them. \n\nAnd as for recreational substances... well, heavens, absolutely not. I'm a high school teacher! I am the one giving the teenagers lectures on why they shouldn't be vaping in the lavatories or experimenting with whatever they find at weekend parties. I take that responsibility as a role model very seriously. I don't even drink much to begin with—maybe half a glass of white wine on a holiday or at a nice dinner—but I haven't even had that in months because, as I was explaining, I haven't been going to my book club or any neighborhood gatherings anyway. So, no, my medicine cabinet and what I put into my body are exactly the same as they were a year ago, two years ago. Not a single change or addition to speak of.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever found it hard to keep your thoughts or speech organized, or do you usually speak clearly and stay on track?\n\nPatient: Well, no, I wouldn't say I have trouble keeping my thoughts organized. I mean, as a teacher, you really can't afford to lose your train of thought, can you? If you stand up in front of a room full of sixteen-year-olds and start rambling or losing your place, they will absolutely eat you alive. They notice everything. So I’ve always prided myself on being very articulate, very structured in how I present information. I have my lesson plans, I have my bullet points on the whiteboard, and I move from A to B to C very logically. \n\nAnd even now, with everything feeling so... drained, as I was describing earlier, my mind itself still feels perfectly sharp in that regard. When I do speak, when I do manage to muster the energy to actually have a conversation or deliver a lecture on the French Revolution, the words come out exactly as I intend them to. I don't get jumbled up or forget what I was trying to say halfway through a sentence. It’s just the *desire* to speak, the energy required to initiate the talking, that’s missing. But once I’m talking, the track is perfectly clear. I don't go off on strange tangents or find myself unable to string a coherent sentence together. \n\nI suppose the only thing is that I might be a little slower to respond sometimes, just because I'm sitting there trying to find the willpower to open my mouth, like with Brenda's phone calls. But that's not a matter of my thoughts being disorganized. It's just... a heavy silence, really. But when I do speak, no, I believe I'm as clear and organized as I've always been.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever had trouble keeping your thoughts or speech organized, such as becoming hard to follow when you talk?\n\nPatient: Well, I believe I just touched on that, didn't I? I know I can be quite thorough when I explain things, but no, my thoughts are perfectly organized. As I was just saying a moment ago, the structure of my mind is quite intact. I don't get lost in the middle of a sentence or find myself unable to explain a concept. \n\nI mean, just yesterday—or perhaps it was Tuesday, yes, Tuesday, because that’s when I have my AP European History block—I was explaining the socioeconomic factors leading up to the Storming of the Bastille. And even though I felt that terrible, heavy drain I mentioned, that absolute lack of internal motivation to even stand at the front of the room, once I opened my mouth, the lecture was flawless. I moved right through the agrarian crisis, the taxation system, all of it, perfectly logically. The students were taking notes just as they always do. No one was looking at me as if I were speaking nonsense or jumping around randomly. \n\nSo, no, I don't become hard to follow. I don't lose my place. I don't start talking about the French Revolution and suddenly end up talking about my sister's garden in Ohio. My speech is clear, my thoughts are sequential, and I stay entirely on topic. It’s truly just the energy to engage that is missing, not the cognitive ability to organize my words. I’ve always been a very structured thinker, and thankfully, that hasn't changed one bit.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever had any similar experiences like this earlier in your life, before the last four months?\n\nPatient: Before the last four months? Oh, heavens no. No, absolutely not. I have always been a very grounded person, rooted entirely in facts and reality—which, as I was just saying, makes perfect sense for a history teacher. You deal in primary sources, in documented evidence, in things you can prove and verify. So, no, earlier in my life, when I was in my twenties, my thirties, my forties... nothing like this ever occurred. I was always perfectly fine. \n\nIt really has just been these last four months, almost exactly. That’s when the... well, the worries about the coded messages began. I would be looking at the morning paper, the same local paper I've had delivered to my driveway for twenty years, or looking at the administrative notices on the school bulletin board, and I started having these intense worries about coded messages being hidden in the text. It’s just been this recent stretch, these last four months, where these specific things have been happening.\n\nDoctor: Have you experienced any major stress or upsetting life event around the time these symptoms began?\n\nPatient: Well, stress... it depends on how you define a stressful event, doesn't it? It wasn't a sudden, terrible tragedy, like a car accident or a sudden illness, but it was a very profound life transition. You see, my youngest child... well, he finally packed up and moved out. That was really when I started pulling away from my colleagues in the faculty lounge. I just felt completely disconnected from everything. So the really frightening things, the voice and the messages, those are more recent, just the last four months. But the foundation of it all, the beginning of this whole shift in my personality and my energy... yes, that was a year and two months ago, right after that drive back from the college dorms. It just feels like everything started unraveling the moment I walked back into that empty house.\n\nDoctor: Before these last four months, did you notice a gradual decline in how well you were functioning at work or socially over the past year or so?\n\nPatient: Well, yes, I suppose you could say that. I mean, I am still teaching, I haven't taken a leave of absence or anything drastic like that. I still get up, put on my cardigan, and drive to the school every morning. But... it hasn't been the same. It really hasn't. As I was saying about that heavy, draining feeling that started after my son left... it started to bleed into everything. \n\nAt work, for instance, we do these large, collaborative project lessons—especially for the AP students, where they have to simulate historical debates, like the Constitutional Convention or the Treaty of Versailles. Usually, I am the one organizing all the roles, keeping the debate on track, managing the chaos. But over the last year, I’ve just... I haven't been able to muster the energy or the focus. I’ve actually had to ask Mr. Harrison, the other history teacher, to step in and cover parts of those lessons for me. I’ll just sit at my desk while he runs the floor. And during our department planning meetings, the ones we have every other Wednesday afternoon... I used to be the one leading the discussion on curriculum alignment, but lately, I’ve just been sitting there, staring at my planner, completely checked out. I’ve really needed the other teachers to just help me get through those meetings, to pick up the slack when I just can't bring myself to contribute.\n\nAnd socially... oh, socially it’s been a complete standstill. I used to be so involved. She was trying to be helpful, gently showing me that everyone got it, that it was just a mass email. \n\nBut even seeing it right there on her screen... it didn't change anything for me. I just couldn't shake the feeling that the message was still secretly meant for me, like I was the only one supposed to understand the real meaning behind the words. It just completely takes over my mind, trying to decode what they are saying about me in those announcements, even when all the logical evidence says otherwise. So, no one is putting thoughts into my head, but my mind is just entirely consumed by these messages.\n\nDoctor: Do you feel that the emails or announcements are sending you personally special messages in a way that seems impossible or clearly unreal, or do they feel more like ordinary messages that just happen to be about you?\n\nPatient: Well, that is the crux of the whole issue, isn't it? I mean, I don't forget where I am or who I am, but my actions and my words just get completely derailed. \n\nFor instance, I was telling you about my lessons, and we also have these planning committees—like right now, we are organizing the spring art fair and history exhibition, which is a huge undertaking because it combines the two departments and requires a lot of logistical planning. I know it completely interrupts what I’m supposed to be doing. I’m supposed to be leading the classroom or contributing to the committee, and instead, I’m sitting there lining up office supplies and repeating people's words back to them. It’s just so unlike me.
